title: Ventricular Septal Defect
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A VSD is a hole in the ventricular septum causing left-to-right shunt. Clinical focus is on size, haemodynamic impact and risk of Eisenmenger. Management balances observation, medical therapy and timely surgery.

sections.p: A VSD is an opening in the interventricular septum allowing blood to flow from the high‑pressure left ventricle to the right ventricle during systole. Diagnosis is clinical plus echocardiography; ECG and chest X‑ray support the assessment.
b: Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal edge
Echocardiography shows defect size, location and shunt direction

t.b: Shows septal anatomy, flow velocity, Qp:Qs ratio; guides management
Enlarged cardiac silhouette indicates significant left‑to‑right shunt
Right‑ventricular strain pattern suggests large VSD

sections.p: Severity is graded by shunt magnitude (Qp:Qs) and clinical impact. Small VSDs (Qp:Qs<1.5) often close spontaneously. Moderate (1.5–2.5) may need intervention; large (>2.5) risk heart failure and Eisenmenger.
Most VSDs are sporadic, but consider maternal rubella, diabetes, alcohol, and teratogens. In low‑resource settings, infections (e.g., HIV, TB) and nutritional deficiencies may increase risk.
Typical features include a harsh pansystolic murmur, bounding pulses, and a wide pulse pressure. Large defects cause failure to thrive, tachypnoea, and recurrent infections.
b: Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal edge

sections.p: Echocardiography is the gold standard. In settings without echo, a bedside Doppler or pulse oximetry may give clues. Lab tests rule out infections.

t.b: Normal in left‑to‑right shunt; low in Eisenmenger
Leucocytosis suggests infection; anaemia may worsen symptoms

sections.p: Urgent signs include severe dyspnoea, cardiomegaly, pulmonary hypertension, and cyanosis. Complications are heart failure, arrhythmia, infective endocarditis, and Eisenmenger syndrome.

Treat underlying causes, provide supportive care (oxygen, diuretics, ACE inhibitors), and plan surgical closure for large or symptomatic defects. Medical therapy is reserved for small, asymptomatic VSDs.

t.b: Reduce afterload and LV volume overload
Symptomatic fluid overload or pulmonary congestion

sections.p: Regular echocardiograms every 6–12 months for moderate VSDs. Counsel parents on infection prevention and avoid herbal remedies that may worsen haemodynamics.
Large VSD mimics aortic regurgitation or tricuspid regurgitation. A pansystolic murmur can also be due to mitral regurgitation.
A normal chest X‑ray does not exclude a moderate VSD; small defects may be missed. Pulse oximetry may remain normal until pulmonary hypertension develops.

faq.q: What is the most common type of VSD?
faq.a: Membranous VSD is the most frequent, located near the aortic and pulmonary valves.

faq.q: Can a VSD close on its own?
faq.a: Yes, small VSDs (<5 mm) often close spontaneously within the first year of life.

faq.q: Why is infective endocarditis prophylaxis recommended?
faq.a: Large VSDs expose the endocardium to high shear stress, increasing risk of bacterial colonisation during invasive procedures.

exam: A 2‑year‑old presents with tachypnoea and a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge. What is the next best investigation? — Echocardiography to assess defect size and shunt magnitude.
A child with a known VSD develops cyanosis and clubbing. What complication is most likely? — Eisenmenger syndrome due to reversed shunt.
During a routine exam you hear a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Mitral regurgitation, not VSD.
A 6‑month‑old with a small VSD is asymptomatic. What is the recommended management? — Observation with serial echocardiograms; no surgery needed.

A patient with a large VSD is started on diuretics. Which drug class is contraindicated in this setting? — Loop diuretics are fine; however, NSAIDs should be avoided due to risk of renal impairment and reduced diuretic efficacy.
A VSD patient is scheduled for surgery but has active malaria infection. What should be done? — Treat malaria first and delay surgery until infection resolves.
